score_objections.objection: Both tech_regulation sources show Wyden resisting new platform regulation: he defends Section 230 against repeal and was one of three no votes on KOSA/COPPA 2.0 (on privacy/encryption/censorship grounds). His pro-regulation moves in this set (Algorithmic Accountability Act, pressing app stores, surveillance limits) cut the other way, so the record here reads as mixed rather than clearly 'Targeted rules'.

None of the 19 items addresses federal preemption of state AI laws. The only state-related item (letter to Oregon's Data Center Advisory Committee) encourages state action on data centers but says nothing about blocking or preserving state AI regulation. Evidence is too thin for a -2 'Let states regulate' assignment.

score_objections.objection: The only evidence is a single clause (Feb 2024) that 'we must consider the effects that AI could have on ... energy use' plus an interview remark that she is interested in energy-efficiency research. Neither states a position on building, pausing, or conditioning data centers, or on ratepayers. Too thin to place her on the scale even at 'Mixed'.

Sources do not support the strongest 'Let states regulate' position. The Matsui letter she signed is explicitly conditional ('least of all when there are no meaningful federal protections in place'), her Jan 2026 statement faults moratorium advocates for failing to offer a national comprehensive proposal (implying a federal framework would be acceptable), and in Feb 2024 she said 'I don't think we can have 50 different systems; I think it needs to be done at the federal level.' Net picture is opposition to preemption absent a federal standard, not a principled preference for state regulation.
